content: Folliculitis refers to the inflammation of one or more hair follicles, which can occur on any part of the skin. It can be classified based on the depth of involvement (superficial or deep), the underlying cause (infectious or non-infectious), and the chronicity of the condition (acute, chronic, or recurrent). Non-infectious variants include pseudofolliculitis barbae, eosinophilic folliculitis, drug-induced acneiform folliculitis, folliculitis decalvans, tufted folliculitis, and acne keloidalis nuchae. Infectious causes may involve bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites, while non-infectious causes can result from follicular trauma, inflammation, occlusion, scratching, or topical steroid use. Eosinophilic folliculitis has an unknown cause but may involve microorganisms like Demodex mites, Pityrosporum yeast, or bacteria, and autoimmune processes have also been investigated. Chronic cases may show granulomatous inflammation with giant cells containing keratin and fragmented hair. Suppurative folliculitis often resolves spontaneously, but long-standing cases may lead to granuloma or fibrosis with scarring. The incidence is difficult to determine as many affected individuals do not seek medical attention. Folliculitis can affect individuals of all age groups. Superficial folliculitis and hot tub folliculitis are more common in adults, while Demodex folliculitis is also seen in children with facial pustules and papules. Superficial folliculitis affects men and women equally, but males are more commonly affected by herpes folliculitis and Pityrosporum folliculitis. Eosinophilic folliculitis has been observed in HIV-infected individuals of all genders and ages. There is no racial predilection for folliculitis, but pseudofolliculitis barbae primarily affects individuals of African descent. Most cases of folliculitis are caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Damage to hair follicles from friction, blockage, or shaving can predispose to infection. Chronic cases may be associated with iron deficiency anemia. Specific types include sycosis barbae, a staph infection in the beard area, often aggravated by shaving, and pseudofolliculitis barbae, which occurs in men of African descent when curly beard hairs grow back into the skin. Hot tub folliculitis is caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa and typically occurs after exposure to improperly cleaned hot tubs, with symptoms appearing on areas submerged in water, such as the legs, hips, and buttocks. Drug-induced folliculitis can result from medications like betamethasone valerate, clocortolone pivalate, and sorafenib. Risk factors for folliculitis include frequent shaving against the direction of hair growth, immunosuppression, dermatosis, long-term oral antibiotic use, tight clothing, poor hygiene, friction, obesity, diabetes, late-stage HIV with low CD4 counts, prolonged topical steroid use, exposure to hot and humid environments, treatment with EGFR inhibitors, and certain vaccinations (e.g., smallpox and anthrax). Most patients with folliculitis are asymptomatic, but some may experience pruritic or painful erythematous papules or pustules. If untreated, folliculitis may progress to furuncles, which can rupture and discharge pus and necrotic material. Complications include cellulitis, furunculosis, scarring, sinus tract formation, permanent hair loss, and recurrence. In individuals with darker skin, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation may occur, taking months to years to resolve. Prognosis is excellent if the causative agent is identified and treated. Diagnosis of folliculitis is primarily clinical, based on history and physical examination. Symptoms include clusters of small red bumps or white-headed pimples around hair follicles, itchy or painful skin lesions, and pus-filled blisters that may crust over. Physical examination may reveal erythematous, folliculocentric papules and pustules, typically less than 5 mm in diameter. Superficial folliculitis presents as small papules and pustules on an erythematous base, while deep folliculitis manifests as tender plaques and nodules that may heal with scarring. Systemic symptoms like fever may occur in deeper or immunocompromised cases. Laboratory tests are generally reserved for treatment-resistant cases. CBC may show leukocytosis and eosinophilia, with elevated IgE levels in eosinophilic folliculitis. Recurrent cases may warrant RBS testing or HIV testing. Gram stain and culture can identify S. aureus, while Pseudomonas species can be cultured from pustules in hot tub folliculitis. Nasal cultures of family members may help identify S. aureus colonization in chronic cases. KOH preparation and fungal culture can diagnose dermatophyte infections, while skin biopsy is useful for visualizing Pityrosporum yeast in Pityrosporum folliculitis. Viral culture, PCR, or immunofluorescence testing can confirm herpes folliculitis. Histological findings vary by causative agent. Eosinophilic folliculitis shows perifollicular infiltrates of lymphocytes and eosinophils with follicular eosinophilic spongiosis. Bacterial and fungal folliculitis show neutrophils infiltrating the follicular walls and lumen, with lymphocytes and macrophages in chronic cases. Viral folliculitis is characterized by lymphocyte infiltration in the follicular walls and lumen. Demodex folliculitis shows perifollicular lymphohistiocytic inflammation with Demodex folliculorum mites in the follicles. Treatment of uncomplicated folliculitis is often self-limiting. Complicated or recurrent cases require targeted therapy. Oral antibiotics for 7–10 days may be needed for resistant cases. Pseudomonas folliculitis can be treated with oral ciprofloxacin in immunocompromised patients. Gram-negative folliculitis, often due to chronic antibiotic use, is managed by discontinuing the implicated antibiotic and administering oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Other therapies include PUVA, topical tacrolimus, and isotretinoin. Fungal folliculitis responds to oral antifungals like fluconazole or itraconazole. Viral folliculitis is treated with valacyclovir, famciclovir, or acyclovir. Antiparasitic agents like permethrin and oral ivermectin are effective for Demodex folliculitis. Surgical excision may be considered for severe cases of folliculitis keloidalis resistant to medical therapy, particularly if lesions are large (>3 cm) or involve fibrotic plaques or nodules. Surgical options include excision with primary closure, skin grafting, or excision with secondary intention healing, which can yield good cosmetic outcomes with minimal recurrence. Carbon dioxide laser excision and electrosurgery followed by secondary intention healing have also been reported. Preventive measures include maintaining good personal hygiene, avoiding tight clothing, not sharing razors, shaving in the direction of hair growth or using an electric razor, avoiding unsanitary hot tubs and pools, and daily decontamination of personal items. A five-day course of topical mupirocin ointment in the nares and daily chlorhexidine body washes can be used for decolonization. Patients should be followed up two weeks after treatment to assess response.
